brief:
Translate the given UI strings from English into ko for a software product.
These are the navigation chrome of a documentation site for a design-asset platform called Lolly: top-nav links, documentation-sidebar group headings and link labels, page titles, and a handful of footer and language-picker labels. They are extremely short - one to four words, occasionally a page title of a dozen - and they must stay that way: a nav bar and a sidebar have a fixed width, and a label that doubles in length wraps or is clipped. Translate each as the label a native reader would expect to click, not as a sentence, and keep any leading or trailing symbol or arrow exactly where it is. Do not translate product, protocol or format names (Lolly, SUSE, CLI, TUI, MCP, C2PA, URL, API, PDF, SVG): several of these labels are already left in English on purpose in the shipped catalogs, and that is the right answer where the term is what the reader searches for.
Register: polite standard speech (해요체) — friendly but respectful UI register, the modern SaaS/app default; not deferential formal speech (하십시오체) and not casual banmal (반말).
Never translate these terms — copy them verbatim wherever they appear: "Lolly", "SUSE", "Geeko", "Content Credentials", "C2PA", "Pose Geeko", "Neurospicy".
Preserve every {placeholder} token exactly (same braces, same name, same count) — these are runtime interpolations, not prose.
Preserve any inline HTML exactly: the same tags, the same count, every attribute (href, target, rel) byte-for-byte, and every HTML entity (&, <). Translate only the human text around and between the tags — never a tag name, an attribute value, or the contents of a <code> element.
Preserve punctuation choices like → and & as-is where they read naturally in the target language; do not add explanatory text.
Match the source length and register. Do not pad or embellish.
Return ONLY the JSON matching the given schema — one translation per input id, in the same order.
